scenarios.title: The five-layer stall
scenarios.situation: A team trains a 5-hidden-layer MLP on tabular data. Hidden layers use sigmoid activations, the loss drops a little in the first epoch, then barely moves for 50 more. Gradients in the first layers are near zero while the last layer still learns.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and the first fix to try?
choices: Saturating activations: sigmoid outputs squash into (0,1) and its derivative peaks at 0.25, so gradients shrink multiplicatively across layers. Replace hidden-layer sigmoids with ReLU (or leaky ReLU), which passes positive gradients through unchanged, and retrain.
The network needs more layers: depth is the only thing that matters, so add three more sigmoid layers.
Raise the learning rate to 0.5: a bigger step will push through the stall.
Switch the optimizer from SGD to Adam first: the optimizer is always the root cause of a stall.
scenarios.why: Sigmoid's maximum derivative of 0.25 compounds layer after layer (0.25^5 is roughly 1/1000), which is the textbook vanishing-gradient setup. ReLU's derivative is 1 for positive inputs, so the signal survives. Optimizer and learning-rate changes treat the symptom; the activation choice is the disease.
scenarios.hint: What is the largest value the sigmoid derivative can take, and what happens when you multiply it five times?

scenarios.title: MSE on a classifier
scenarios.situation: A 10-class image classifier ends in a softmax layer but is trained with MSELoss against one-hot targets. After 20 epochs accuracy sits near 10% — chance level — while the loss looks small and flat. The data pipeline checks out.
scenarios.prompt: What should change?
choices: Replace MSELoss with CrossEntropyLoss applied to the raw logits (drop the final softmax layer — CrossEntropyLoss includes log-softmax). MSE on softmax outputs gives weak, flat gradients for confident-wrong predictions and is not the right probabilistic objective for classification.
Normalize the input images more aggressively: the pixel scale is the problem.
Train for 200 more epochs: MSE just needs more time on classification.
Add dropout 0.5: the model is overfitting, which is why accuracy is low.
scenarios.why: Cross-entropy penalizes confident-wrong predictions with steep gradients (the gradient is simply predicted probability minus one-hot target), while MSE on softmax saturates. Also note CrossEntropyLoss expects logits, so keeping an explicit softmax before it double-squashes the outputs — a classic shape bug.
scenarios.hint: For a confidently wrong prediction, which loss gives the stronger correction signal — squared error on a probability, or negative log-likelihood?

scenarios.title: The frozen early layers
scenarios.situation: A 30-layer MLP trains on a regression task. Loss plateaus early. Weight histograms show the last few layers changing every epoch while the first ten layers are nearly frozen. Initialization was the default uniform, activations are tanh.
scenarios.prompt: How do you diagnose and fix this?
choices: Diagnose vanishing gradients: with tanh saturating and naive initialization, the signal decays before reaching early layers. Fix with He or Xavier initialization matched to the activation, ReLU-family activations, and batch normalization or residual skip connections so gradients have a short path.
Train ten times longer: deep networks just need more epochs for the signal to arrive.
Increase the batch size to 4096: bigger batches push gradients deeper.
Add strong L2 weight decay: regularization will unfreeze the early layers.
scenarios.why: This is the depth pathology: each layer multiplies the gradient by the activation derivative and the weights, and tanh saturates at derivative ~0. Skip connections give the gradient an express lane (the core ResNet insight), batch norm stabilizes layer input distributions, and matched initialization keeps the initial signal scale sane.
scenarios.hint: If the last layers learn and the first do not, where is the gradient dying — and what architectural shortcut could bypass the long chain?

scenarios.title: Two thousand images
scenarios.situation: A team has 2,000 labeled defect images and trains a ResNet-50 from scratch. Training accuracy hits 99% by epoch 3 while validation accuracy stalls at 61%. They propose labeling 50,000 more images before trying again.
scenarios.prompt: What is the better engineering call?
choices: Use transfer learning: start from ImageNet-pretrained weights, freeze the backbone, train only the classifier head with augmentation, then optionally unfreeze later layers with a small learning rate. The pretrained filters already encode edges, textures, and shapes — 2,000 images cannot learn those from scratch.
Label the 50,000 images first: from-scratch training is the only honest approach.
Switch to a larger model: capacity is what a small dataset needs.
Early stopping alone will fix it: just stop at epoch 2.
scenarios.why: Early visual features are largely task-agnostic, so borrowing them is not cheating — it is the standard practice for small datasets. Freezing the backbone first prevents the small dataset from destroying good features; augmentation multiplies the effective data. Labeling 50k images burns months to relearn what the pretrained model already knows.
scenarios.hint: Which parts of a vision network are most reusable across tasks — the early filters or the final classifier — and what does that imply for a 2,000-image dataset?

scenarios.title: The haunted evaluation
scenarios.situation: At inference time the same input image gets a different predicted class on repeated runs. The team suspects data corruption, then a bad checkpoint, then a hardware fault. The model file loads fine and training metrics were stable.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The model was never switched out of training mode: dropout layers are still randomly zeroing activations and batch-norm layers are using batch statistics. Call model.eval() before inference (and wrap it in torch.no_grad()), which disables dropout and freezes batch-norm to its running statistics.
Set a manual seed before every prediction: nondeterminism is always a seeding problem.
Batch normalization is broken and must be removed from the architecture.
Reload the checkpoint before each prediction: the weights are decaying in memory.
scenarios.why: Dropout is only meant to be active during training — that is its entire design. model.train()/model.eval() is a global mode switch, not a per-layer setting, and forgetting it is one of the most common production bugs in PyTorch. torch.no_grad() additionally skips autograd bookkeeping, which speeds inference and cuts memory.
scenarios.hint: Which layers behave differently in training versus inference — and is there a single call that flips them all?

scenarios.title: The diverging curves
scenarios.situation: Training loss falls steadily for 40 epochs while validation loss bottoms out at epoch 12 and then climbs. The team debates: train longer with a lower learning rate, or add two more hidden layers to 'give the model room to generalize.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct read and response?
choices: This is overfitting: the model is memorizing training noise after epoch 12. Stop there — use early stopping on validation loss — and regularize: dropout, weight decay, or augmentation. More capacity or more epochs will make the gap worse, not better.
Train longer with a lower learning rate: the validation curve just needs patience.
Add the two hidden layers: underfitting is the real problem.
Delete the validation set and train on all the data: the split is causing the gap.
scenarios.why: The validation curve is the honest reporter: once it rises while training loss falls, every extra epoch is memorization. Early stopping converts that observation into policy (save the best-validation checkpoint). Regularization attacks the cause — excess effective capacity — instead of feeding it.
scenarios.hint: If training loss keeps improving while validation loss worsens, is the model learning the task or the dataset — and which curve should decide when to stop?

scenarios.title: The Shape Mismatch
scenarios.situation: A ResNet-style model crashes with a tensor shape error at the first skip connection. The block downsamples spatially but the identity path doesn't match.
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard fix for dimension mismatch in residual connections?
choices: Add a 1x1 convolution (projection shortcut) on the identity path to match dimensions — the standard ResNet solution
Remove the skip connection — it's optional
Pad the smaller tensor with zeros — simplest fix
Change the main path to not downsample — keep dimensions constant
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. When F(x) changes dimensions (spatial downsampling or channel increase), the identity x can't be added directly. The ResNet paper's solution: a 1x1 conv projection on the shortcut to match shapes. Zero-padding works for channels but not spatial; removing skips defeats the purpose; avoiding downsampling cripples the architecture.
scenarios.hint: What are the two things that must match for element-wise addition?
evidence: RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (56) must match the size of tensor b (28) at non-singleton dimension 3
Main path: conv stride=2 (56→28). Shortcut: identity (still 56).

lessons.title: Deep Learning with PyTorch — Core concepts
concepts: A perceptron is a weighted sum plus a bias; stacking them into a multilayer network only gains power because nonlinear activations sit between layers — without them the whole stack collapses to one linear map.
Match the loss to the task: cross-entropy on raw logits for classification, mean squared error for regression. The loss defines what 'wrong' costs, so a mismatched loss teaches the wrong lesson.

Backpropagation is the chain rule applied mechanically: every operation records how its output changes with its inputs, and gradients flow backward through that recorded graph. PyTorch's autograd builds the graph for you — your job is to design it honestly.

The optimizer and learning rate matter more than architecture tweaks: SGD with momentum and Adam are the workhorses, and the learning rate (plus a schedule that decays it) is the single highest-leverage knob. Too large diverges; too small stalls.

Convolutions share weights across space, which buys translation equivariance and far fewer parameters than dense layers; pooling and stride downsample. For small datasets, transfer learning from a pretrained backbone beats training from scratch.

Regularize as a triad, not a lottery ticket: dropout (disable at eval), weight decay (L2 on the optimizer), and early stopping on validation loss. Tune everything on validation — the test set is read once, at the end.

example.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim=20, hidden=64, n_classes=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(in_dim, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.2),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, n_classes),  # raw logits out
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

model = MLP().to(device)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()          # expects logits
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X, y), batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

best_val, patience = float("inf"), 0
for epoch in range(50):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in loader:
        xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()              # clear stale gradients
        loss = criterion(model(xb), yb)
        loss.backward()                    # autograd fills .grad
        optimizer.step()                   # SGD/Adam update
    val_loss = evaluate(model, val_loader, device)  # uses model.eval() + no_grad()
    if val_loss < best_val:
        best_val, patience = val_loss, 0
        torch.save(model.state_dict(), "best.pt")  # checkpoint the best, not the last
    else:
        patience += 1
        if patience >= 5:
            break  # early stopping
example.walkthrough: This is the canonical PyTorch training loop, and every production trainer is a variation of it. Device discipline comes first: the model and every batch move to the same device, or you get a device-mismatch error. Each batch zeroes old gradients (PyTorch accumulates them by default), runs forward, computes the loss on logits, backpropagates, and steps the optimizer. The validation pass runs under model.eval() with torch.no_grad() so dropout is off and no graph is built. The checkpoint saves only the best-validation state_dict — early stopping as executable policy, not a slogan.

pitfalls: Common trap: calling CrossEntropyLoss on softmax outputs — it expects raw logits and applies log-softmax internally, so a manual softmax double-squashes them.
Common trap: forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() — gradients accumulate across batches by default, so the update silently uses stale gradient history.
Common trap: evaluating with the model still in train mode — dropout stays active and predictions go nondeterministic (see scenario 5).
Common trap: tuning on the test set — every peek leaks information; the test set is read exactly once, after all decisions are frozen.

Tab completion, command history (up/down arrows), and 'help' work as expected — treat it like a real shell.

Mistakes are safe here: the simulated environment resets, and there's no production system to break.
Many interviewers ask candidates to live-demo commands — practicing here builds that muscle memory.
The 'try_it' prompt at the end of lessons often points to a terminal exercise — do it immediately while the concept is fresh.

$ help              # list available commands
$ ls                # list current directory
$ cd <dir>         # change directory

Skipping terminal exercises because 'I understand the concept' — doing wires it differently than reading.
Fear of breaking something — this is a sandbox; experiment freely.

lessons.title: Capstone: Neural Network Project — Project Brief
concepts: Your capstone: a complete deep learning project: custom architecture trained on real data with proper evaluation
Why a capstone matters: interviewers remember stories about things you built far longer than quiz scores. This is your proof.
Build in public: commit early, commit often. A git history showing iterative progress impresses more than a perfect final upload.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason in the README. Future-you (and interviewers) will thank present-you.
Scope discipline: a finished small project beats an abandoned ambitious one. The milestones below are sized to complete.
Demo readiness: you must be able to screen-share this project and narrate every part in under 5 minutes.

example.code:
Neural Network Project — Milestones:

  1. Dataset preparation & augmentation pipeline
  2. Custom model architecture
  3. Training loop with callbacks & checkpointing
  4. Evaluation, visualization & deployment

Each milestone is independently demoable.
Finish one before starting the next.
example.walkthrough: Create your project repo today — even if it's just a README with the milestone list. Momentum starts with the first commit.

pitfalls: Gold-plating milestone 1 while milestones 4-5 remain untouched — timebox each milestone.
Building without documenting — an undocumented project is nearly worthless as a portfolio piece.
Waiting until it's 'ready' to commit — commit the skeleton now; iterate in the open.
lessons.try_it: Create the repo and README for Neural Network Project now. Write the milestone list and your 'why' for each.

lessons.title: Capstone: Neural Network Project — Build Guide
concepts: Milestone 1 — Foundation: scaffold the project, verify the toolchain works end-to-end before adding complexity.
Milestone 2 — Core: implement the central functionality. This is the demoable heart of the project.
Milestone 3 — Hardening: handle errors, add validation, make it robust enough to demo without fear.
Milestone 4 — Polish: README, diagrams, clean output. This is what separates 'homework' from 'portfolio'.
Testing each milestone: define 'done' as a verifiable behavior, not a feeling. Write the check before the code.
Narrative prep: for each milestone, prepare a 60-second explanation — what it does, why it matters, what was hard.

example.code:
Definition of done (example, Milestone 2):

  ✓ Core feature works with valid input
  ✓ Graceful error on invalid input
  ✓ Output verified against expected result
  ✓ Committed with a clear message
  ✓ README section updated

No milestone is done until all boxes check.
example.walkthrough: Work milestone 1 today. When every 'done' box checks, commit and move on. Resist the urge to perfect.

pitfalls: Skipping the hardening milestone — demos fail live, and robustness is what interviewers probe.
No verifiable 'done' criteria — 'it works on my machine' is not done.
Building all milestones before testing any — integrate and verify incrementally.
lessons.try_it: Complete milestone 1 of your capstone. Verify every 'done' box before moving on.

lessons.title: Capstone: Neural Network Project — Demo & Interview Prep
concepts: The 5-minute demo arc: problem (30s) → approach (60s) → live walkthrough (2.5min) → lessons learned (60s).
Anticipate the deep questions: 'Why did you choose X over Y?' 'What breaks at scale?' 'What would you do differently?'
Resume bullet formula: Action verb + what you built + tech + measurable outcome. Quantify everything you can.
LinkedIn/portfolio: screenshots or a 60-second screen recording outperform text descriptions 10:1.
Bring the repo to interviews: offer to walk through the code. Few candidates do this — it signals genuine ownership.
Post-mortem: write 5 lines on what you'd improve. Interviewers love candidates who can critique their own work.

Resume bullet:
  'Built {proj} processing [N] records with [tech];
   reduced [metric] by [X]% via [technique].'

Demo opener:
  'The problem: [one sentence].
   My approach: [one sentence].
   Let me show you...'

pitfalls: Demoing without a narrative — clicking around silently while the interviewer watches is painful.
No answer for 'what would you do differently' — always have one; it shows growth mindset.
Portfolio link rot — verify every link on your resume actually works before submitting.
lessons.try_it: Record a 60-second screen share of your current progress. Watch it back — is the narrative clear?

lessons.title: Perceptrons & Activation Functions
concepts: A perceptron is a weighted sum plus a nonlinearity — every neural network is stacks of these
Activation functions break linearity: without them, 100 layers collapse to one linear transform
ReLU dominates hidden layers: cheap, sparse, avoids vanishing gradients — but watch for dead neurons
Sigmoid/tanh belong to outputs (probabilities) and gates (LSTMs) — not hidden layers in deep nets

example.code:
z = w·x + b
a = max(0, z)   # ReLU
# deep net = a₃(W₃·a₂(W₂·a₁(W₁·x))) — nesting, not magic
example.walkthrough: Implement a perceptron from scratch with NumPy. Train it on AND/OR, then watch it fail on XOR — that's why we need hidden layers.

pitfalls: Using sigmoid in deep hidden layers — vanishing gradients stall training
Forgetting the bias term — the network can't shift the activation threshold
No nonlinearity between layers — you've built expensive linear regression
lessons.try_it: Build a 2-layer MLP from scratch that solves XOR. Plot the decision boundary.

lessons.title: Backpropagation from First Principles
concepts: Backprop is just the chain rule applied systematically — gradients flow backward through each operation
The forward pass computes values; the backward pass computes how each parameter should change
Gradient = direction of steepest increase; we step opposite for minimization — that's all gradient descent is
Vanishing/exploding gradients: products of many small/large numbers — the reason for careful init and normalization

example.code:
# scalar chain rule
dL/dw = dL/da · da/dz · dz/dw
# each layer multiplies by its local gradient
# deep chains → products → vanish or explode
example.walkthrough: Derive the gradient for a single neuron by hand. Then verify with numerical gradients (finite differences).

pitfalls: Treating backprop as magic — you must be able to derive a simple case
Ignoring gradient norms during training — log them; sudden spikes predict divergence
Wrong reduction on batched gradients — mean vs sum changes your effective learning rate
lessons.try_it: Implement manual backprop for a 2-layer net and match PyTorch autograd to 1e-5.

lessons.title: Convolutions: Learning Spatial Features
concepts: Convolution = sliding a learned filter across the image, computing dot products — detecting local patterns everywhere
Weight sharing: one filter applied everywhere means far fewer parameters than dense layers on images
Hierarchical features: early layers learn edges, middle learn textures/parts, deep learn objects — emergent, not programmed
Padding preserves size ('same'), stride downsamples; pooling adds translation invariance cheaply

example.code:
nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=64,
           kernel_size=3, padding=1)  # 3x3x3x64 + bias
# params: 1,792 — vs 150k+ for dense on 224x224
example.walkthrough: Visualize first-layer filters of a pretrained ResNet. Identify edge detectors vs color blob detectors.

pitfalls: Flattening images into dense layers — parameter explosion and no spatial priors
Wrong padding math — output size surprises break skip connections
Aggressive early pooling — destroying spatial detail the network needs later
lessons.try_it: Compute the receptive field of a 3-layer CNN by hand. Verify with a gradient-based visualization.

lessons.title: Modern Architectures: ResNet & Beyond
concepts: Residual connections (skip connections) let gradients flow directly — enabling 100+ layer networks
The residual block learns F(x) = H(x) - x: it's easier to learn a residual than a full mapping
BatchNorm stabilizes training by normalizing layer inputs — but it has train/test behavior differences
Transfer learning: pretrained backbones + new head beats training from scratch on small data, almost always

example.code:
y = F(x) + x   # residual: gradient flows via +x untouched
# without skip: gradient *= many small numbers → vanishes
example.walkthrough: Fine-tune a pretrained ResNet on a small custom dataset. Compare against training from scratch — note the gap.

pitfalls: Freezing nothing when fine-tuning on tiny data — catastrophic forgetting of useful features
BatchNorm in eval mode forgotten — train/test metric mismatch mystery
Reinventing architectures before trying transfer learning — waste of compute
lessons.try_it: Ablate: remove skip connections from a small ResNet. Train both. Document what happens to gradient norms.

lessons.title: Attention Is All You Need
concepts: Attention computes weighted averages where the weights are learned similarities — 'what should I look at?'
Q/K/V: queries ask, keys advertise, values deliver — attention = softmax(QK^T/√d)V
Multi-head attention learns different relationship types in parallel — syntax, coreference, position
Positional encodings inject order since attention is permutation-invariant — without them, sequences are bags

example.code:
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
# QK^T: every position scores every other position
# softmax → weights sum to 1; V weighted by relevance
example.walkthrough: Implement scaled dot-product attention from scratch. Verify the output shape and that rows of weights sum to 1.

pitfalls: Forgetting the √d_k scale — large dot products saturate softmax, killing gradients
No causal mask in decoders — the model cheats by attending to the future
Treating attention weights as explanations — they're not reliably interpretable
lessons.try_it: Visualize attention heads on a sentence. Find one head that tracks syntax (e.g., verb→subject).

lessons.title: Optimizers: Beyond Vanilla SGD
concepts: SGD + momentum: velocity accumulates consistent directions, damps oscillation — the workhorse baseline
Adam adapts per-parameter learning rates using gradient moments — fast, but can generalize slightly worse than SGD
Learning rate is the most important hyperparameter — schedule it: warmup, decay, or cosine annealing
Weight decay (L2) belongs in the optimizer, not the loss — AdamW fixes Adam's incorrect decay

example.code:
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4,
                        weight_decay=0.01)
sched = CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=epochs)
example.walkthrough: Train the same model with SGD+momentum vs Adam. Compare final accuracy AND the loss curves' shapes.

pitfalls: Default lr=1e-3 for everything — Adam's default is a starting point, not a law
No learning rate schedule on long training runs — leaving performance on the table
Tuning the optimizer before the data pipeline is clean — garbage in, fancy optimizer out
lessons.try_it: Run an LR range test: sweep lr exponentially, plot loss. Pick the lr at the steepest descent.

lessons.title: Generalization: The Real Goal
concepts: Training loss is not the goal — validation performance is; the gap between them is overfitting
Dropout randomly zeroes activations during training — an ensemble of subnetworks, cheap
Data augmentation is the highest-ROI regularization for vision — more diverse data beats cleverer models
Early stopping on validation loss is free regularization — always use it

example.code:
nn.Dropout(p=0.5)  # train: zero 50%, scale rest by 2
                # eval: identity (model.eval()!)
# forgetting model.eval() is the classic dropout bug
example.walkthrough: Train with and without augmentation. Plot train/val curves for both — see the generalization gap shrink.

pitfalls: Evaluating with dropout still on — model.eval() forgotten, metrics mysteriously bad
Augmentation leaking into validation — val must reflect real deployment data
Regularizing before establishing a baseline — you can't fix what you haven't measured
lessons.try_it: Design an augmentation pipeline for your data. Justify each transform as 'plausible in deployment'.

lessons.title: PyTorch: Tensors & Autograd
concepts: Everything is a tensor with requires_grad — autograd builds the computation graph dynamically as you compute
loss.backward() populates .grad; optimizer.step() updates; optimizer.zero_grad() clears — forget zero_grad and gradients accumulate silently
model.train() vs model.eval() switches dropout/BatchNorm behavior — wrong mode = wrong results
torch.no_grad() for inference — saves memory and prevents graph buildup

example.code:
for x, y in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()  # the canonical 4-line loop
example.walkthrough: Train a small model. Intentionally forget zero_grad() once — observe the exploding updates. Then fix it.

pitfalls: Forgetting zero_grad() — gradients accumulate across batches, training diverges
Calling .backward() twice without retain_graph — runtime error or wrong grads
Leaving model in train mode during eval — BatchNorm/dropout corrupt metrics
lessons.try_it: Implement gradient clipping in the training loop. Log gradient norms per step.

lessons.title: Detection & Segmentation
concepts: Classification: 'what is in this image?' Detection: 'what and where?' (boxes) Segmentation: 'what at every pixel?'
Two-stage (R-CNN family): propose regions, then classify — accurate, slower. Single-stage (YOLO): direct — fast
IoU (Intersection over Union) measures box quality; mAP averages precision across IoU thresholds and classes
Segmentation with U-Net: encoder downsamples, decoder upsamples, skip connections preserve detail

example.code:
# detection output per image:
# [x1, y1, x2, y2, class, confidence] × N boxes
# NMS removes overlapping duplicates by IoU
example.walkthrough: Run a pretrained YOLO on sample images. Vary the confidence threshold — observe the precision/recall tradeoff.

pitfalls: Evaluating detection with classification accuracy — wrong metric family entirely
Ignoring class imbalance — the model learns 'background' and stops
No NMS tuning — hundreds of overlapping boxes in output
lessons.try_it: Annotate 20 images for a custom class. Fine-tune a detector and report mAP@0.5.

lessons.title: Embeddings & Language Models
concepts: Embeddings map discrete tokens to continuous vectors where similarity = meaning proximity
Pretraining (masked LM / next-token) learns general language; fine-tuning adapts to your task
Tokenization matters: BPE/subword handles open vocabulary — but watch for weird splits on domain text
Context window limits what the model sees — chunk long documents strategically, don't just truncate

example.code:
tokens = tokenizer('Deep learning is powerful',
                    return_tensors='pt')
# input_ids: [101, 2784, 2364, 2003, ...] — subword pieces
example.walkthrough: Compare embeddings of synonyms vs antonyms vs random words using cosine similarity. Sanity-check the space.

pitfalls: Using raw pretrained embeddings without fine-tuning and expecting task performance
Truncating long documents silently — losing the answer-containing chunk
Ignoring tokenization artifacts on domain-specific text
lessons.try_it: Fine-tune a small transformer on a classification task. Compare frozen vs unfrozen backbone.

lessons.title: GANs, VAEs & Diffusion
concepts: VAEs: encoder → latent distribution → decoder; the KL term regularizes the latent space for sampling
GANs: generator vs discriminator in a minimax game — powerful but unstable (mode collapse is the classic failure)
Diffusion: gradually denoise from pure noise — stable training, state-of-the-art quality, slower sampling
Evaluation is hard: FID measures distribution similarity; human eval still matters for perceptual quality

example.code:
# diffusion sampling (simplified)
# x_T ~ N(0, I)  (pure noise)
# for t in reversed(range(T)):
#     x_{t-1} = model(x_t, t)  (denoise one step)
example.walkthrough: Train a tiny VAE on MNIST. Interpolate between two latent codes — observe smooth morphing (the latent space working).

pitfalls: Judging generative models by training loss alone — loss ≠ sample quality
GAN mode collapse unnoticed — check sample diversity, not just sharpness
No fixed evaluation set — cherry-picking best samples as 'results'
lessons.try_it: Implement latent interpolation for a VAE. Document where the space is smooth vs discontinuous.

lessons.title: Serving Deep Learning Models
concepts: Export to ONNX/TorchScript for serving — training frameworks are too heavy for production
Batching requests amortizes GPU cost; dynamic batching balances latency vs throughput
Quantization (FP16/INT8) cuts latency and memory — usually with negligible accuracy loss
Version models like code: registry, staging, canary — never overwrite production blindly

example.code:
# export
torch.onnx.export(model, dummy_input, 'model.onnx')
# serve with ONNX Runtime / Triton — 2-5x faster than PyTorch
example.walkthrough: Export a trained model to ONNX. Benchmark PyTorch vs ONNX Runtime latency on the same inputs.

pitfalls: Serving the training checkpoint directly — slow, bloated, unsafe
No input validation at serving time — adversarial or malformed inputs crash the service
Ignoring GPU memory fragmentation on long-running servers
lessons.try_it: Build a minimal FastAPI service around an ONNX model. Load-test it and report p99 latency.

labs.title: Train an MLP from scratch on synthetic data
labs.objective: Build a two-hidden-layer MLP in PyTorch, train it on a synthetic binary classification set, and report train vs validation accuracy with a clean device-disciplined loop.
steps: Create lab1.py: generate 2,000 samples with sklearn.datasets.make_moons(noise=0.2), split 80/20 with train_test_split, and wrap both splits in TensorDataset/DataLoader.
Define an nn.Module MLP: Linear(2,64) → ReLU → Dropout(0.2) → Linear(64,64) → ReLU → Linear(64,2) with raw-logit output.
Write the training loop with device discipline (.to(device) for model and batches), Adam(lr=1e-3), CrossEntropyLoss, and optimizer.zero_grad() each batch.
Add validation under model.eval() + torch.no_grad(), early stopping with patience 5, and checkpoint the best-validation state_dict to best.pt.
Run for up to 50 epochs, reload best.pt, and print final train and validation accuracy to four decimals.
In two sentences, note whether the curves show underfit, good fit, or overfit — and which regularizer you would reach for first.

checks.hint: Print lines like 'train acc 0.XXXX / val acc 0.XXXX' so the check can see both metrics.

labs.title: Transfer learning with a frozen backbone
labs.objective: Fine-tune a pretrained ResNet-18 on a small image classification task by freezing the backbone, training a new head, then unfreezing with a small learning rate — and measure what each stage buys.
steps: Create lab2.py: load torchvision.models.resnet18 with pretrained weights and replace its fc layer with a new Linear head for your class count.
Stage 1: freeze all backbone parameters (requires_grad=False), train only the head for 5 epochs with Adam(lr=1e-3), and record validation accuracy.
Stage 2: unfreeze the last residual block, retrain the whole net for 5 more epochs with Adam(lr=1e-4), and record validation accuracy again.
Add transforms-based augmentation (random horizontal flip, random crop) to the training loader and re-run Stage 1 — compare the three numbers.
Print all three validation accuracies and, in three sentences, explain which stage helped most and why frozen features transfer.

checks.hint: Print one line per stage, e.g. 'stage1-frozen val acc 0.XXXX', so the check can compare them.

labs.title: Debug the haunted evaluation loop
labs.objective: Find and fix the train/eval-mode bug in a provided broken inference script, proving with repeated runs that predictions become deterministic.
steps: Open broken_eval.py (provided): it loads a trained MLP with dropout, runs inference on 20 held-out samples, and prints predictions — run it three times and record how many predictions change between runs.

Fix the script: switch the model to evaluation mode before the inference loop and disable autograd for the forward passes.
Re-run three times and confirm zero predictions change across runs; print a before/after count of changed predictions.

simulations.title: Loss goes NaN at epoch 3
simulations.brief: The training run is healthy for two epochs, then the loss explodes to NaN at epoch 3. The run is dead — diagnose it.

steps.symptom: Loss NaN at epoch 3 after two healthy epochs.
evidence: Epoch 1: 2.1, epoch 2: 340, epoch 3 (first batches): 1.2e7 — then NaN
Adam, learning rate 0.1, no gradient clipping
Mixed precision enabled; loss scaler overflowed 40 times in epoch 2
options: Lower the learning rate and enable gradient clipping, then resume from the epoch-2 checkpoint
Switch to full float32 precision and keep the learning rate
Increase the batch size to smooth the gradients
Restart training from scratch with the same config — NaNs are random
steps.explain: Gradient norms exploding 1e6x across two epochs is gradient explosion: lr 0.1 is far too hot and nothing clips the updates. Mixed precision just made the overflow visible sooner. Lower the LR, clip gradients, resume from the last good checkpoint.

simulations.debrief: NaN is never random. Read the gradient norms: explosion means the learning rate is too hot or clipping is missing. Fix the cause, resume from the last healthy checkpoint — never restart blind.

steps.symptom: GPU at 8% utilization, epoch takes 4x longer than estimated.
evidence: Training images read from a spinning disk over NFS, one file at a time
0.9s data loading per batch vs 0.1s compute per batch
options: Raise DataLoader workers, enable pin_memory, and move the dataset to fast local storage
Buy a second GPU to parallelize the slow training
Reduce the batch size so each batch loads faster
Switch the model to half precision to speed up compute
steps.explain: Compute takes 0.1s and loading takes 0.9s — the GPU starves while the CPU fetches data serially. Workers parallelize loading, pin_memory speeds host-to-device transfer, local SSD removes the NFS bottleneck. The GPU was never the problem.

simulations.debrief: Low GPU utilization is a data-pipeline diagnosis, not a model problem. Profile the batch time split first: when loading dwarfs compute, fix workers, pinning, and storage before touching the model.

steps.text: 8,000 images, one GPU, image classification. Architecture?

choices.label: Pretrained ResNet with transfer learning — freeze the backbone, train the head
choices.feedback: Correct: transfer learning brings millions of images of prior knowledge. With 8,000 images you fine-tune, not reinvent vision.

choices.label: Train a vision transformer from scratch on the 8,000 images
choices.feedback: Transformers are data-hungry; 8,000 images will not train one from scratch. You would overfit long before the model learns edges.

simulations.debrief: Match the architecture to the data budget: small labeled sets get transfer learning; from-scratch training is for data you do not have. Pretrained backbones are the default, not the shortcut.

cheatsheet: model.train() before training loops; model.eval() + torch.no_grad() before inference — every time.
optimizer.zero_grad() each batch: PyTorch accumulates gradients by default.
nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits; nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss for multi-label; nn.MSELoss for regression.
Device discipline: model.to(device) and every batch .to(device) — mismatched devices raise at runtime.
Checkpoint the best-validation state_dict with torch.save / torch.load, not the last epoch.
DataLoader: shuffle=True for train, False for val; num_workers>0 to stop the GPU starving.
Learning rate first, architecture second: try 1e-3 / 3e-4 / 1e-4 before redesigning the net.
ReLU (or leaky ReLU) in hidden layers by default; saturating activations only where the math demands them.
glossary: tensor
PyTorch's n-dimensional array; the unit of data and parameters, tracked by autograd when requires_grad is set.
autograd
PyTorch's automatic differentiation engine: records operations into a graph and computes gradients via loss.backward().
epoch
One full pass over the training dataset.
batch
The subset of data processed in one optimizer step; batch size trades gradient noise against memory and speed.
learning rate
Step-size multiplier on the gradient update — the highest-leverage hyperparameter.
overfitting
Memorizing training noise: training loss falls while validation loss rises.
underfitting
The model lacks capacity or training to capture even the training signal.
dropout
Regularizer that randomly zeroes activations during training; disabled in eval mode.
weight decay
L2 penalty on weights, usually set on the optimizer; shrinks weights toward zero.
batch normalization
Layer that normalizes its inputs per mini-batch; has distinct train/eval behavior.
convolution
Weight-sharing operation over local neighborhoods; gives translation equivariance with few parameters.
stride / pooling
Downsampling mechanisms that shrink spatial dimensions and grow receptive fields.
transfer learning
Reusing a pretrained backbone's features for a new task, usually by training a new head first.
fine-tuning
Continuing training of some or all pretrained weights on the target task, typically with a small learning rate.
RNN
Recurrent network that carries a hidden state across sequence steps; suffers vanishing gradients over long spans.
LSTM / GRU
Gated recurrent units whose input/forget/output gates let information persist across long sequences.
vanishing gradient
Gradients shrinking toward zero as they propagate through many layers or time steps, freezing early parameters.
gradient clipping
Capping gradient norms before the optimizer step; standard stabilizer for recurrent training.
checkpoint
Saved model state (usually state_dict) allowing training to resume or the best model to be restored.
early stopping
Halting training when validation loss stops improving; the simplest effective regularizer.
